newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea sees drawn out tug-of-war over peace talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea sees drawn out tug-of-war over peace talks.

text.p: South Korean diplomats were flying home from New York on Tuesday with no clear-cut answer from Pyongyang on whether it will join landmark peace talks but not surprised at the tortuous progress of discussions so far.

Officials in Seoul insisted the delegation was not returning empty-handed, since North Korea for the first time had offered an encouraging response to a proposal for the four-way talks, also involving the United States and China.
They said they had expected a diplomatic tug-of-war but remained hopeful the troubled Stalinist regime would eventually agree to talk peace.
South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said discussions over the year-old proposal for talks hit a "temporary impasse" because North Korea had set preconditions.
"We regret the North did not accept the proposal but it was not a big disappointment," he told Reuters.
Many officials and analysts in Seoul believe the North does not want talks with the capitalist South but threats of famine and economic collapse had forced it to the dialogue table.

In the past few days, senior U.S. and South Korean diplomats have tried to secure North Korea's response aimed at securing a lasting peace accord to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
The war sealed the division of the Korean peninsula split at the end of World War Two.
"We had expected a temporary impasse to crop up any time," Lee said. "Even if the North accepts the peace talks, an unexpected variable will probably emerge."

Last Wednesday, the first anniversary of the talks offer by U.S. President Bill Clinton and his South Korean counterpart, Kim Young-sam, Pyongyang indicated it would accept but then tied acceptance to demands for additional food aid and easing of U.S. trade sanctions.
North Korean delegates have since then kept rearranging senior-level meetings, saying they were awaiting directions from home.

North Korean chief delegate Kim Gye-gwan told South Korean and U.S. representatives on Sunday he had spoken to Pyongyang but repeated the earlier demands for assistance and the lifting of a U.S. embargo throttling its economy, Lee said.
A senior official at Seoul's Unification Ministry said a peace treaty with South Korea would mean a dramatic about-face for Pyongyang.
"The North has demanded sacrifices from its citizens for the cause of Korean reunification through communist revolution. A peaceful coexistence would destroy the argument," he said.
"We will have to force North Korea to take steps for peace that it does not want by itself," he said. "North Korea is desperate for food and time is on our side."
Lee said Seoul would not budge from the principle that substantial food aid to North Korea should be discussed only after Pyongyang sits down to peace talks.
"Large-scale food aid can be discussed as part of steps to reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula," he added.
But a Unification Ministry spokesman said South Korea would continue to contribute to humanitarian appeals by international bodies, such as the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP).
South Korea and the United States have pledged $6 million and $25 million respectively to the latest WFP aid appeal for the famine-hit North.
Seoul officials have said South Korea will donate another $10 million or so but the exact amount has yet to be decided.
